items.prose: A fair four-sided die, faces 1 to 4, and a fair six-sided die are rolled together. An outcome is the pair $(f, s)$: $f$ on the four-sided die and $s$ on the six-sided die.

parts.question: How many outcomes are in the sample space $S$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each face of one die pairs with every face of the other.

byKey.added: You added the faces. Each face of one die pairs with every face of the other, so multiply.
byKey.two-sixes: That is two six-sided dice. One die here has only 4 faces.

explain.text: Each of the 4 faces of $f$ pairs with each of the 6 faces of $s$. So $|S| = 4 \times 6 = 24$, all equally likely.

parts.question: Using $|S| = 24$, what is $P(s > f)$, the chance the six-sided die shows more? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: For $f = 1, 2, 3, 4$ the six-sided die wins on $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14$ faces, so $\tfrac{14}{24} = \tfrac{7}{12}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. For each value of $f$, count the faces of $s$ above it.

byKey.ties-in: You counted the ties as wins, 18 outcomes. On a tie neither die shows more.
byKey.thirty-six: You divided by 36. This sample space has 24 outcomes.
byKey.half: You assumed each die is as likely to win. The six-sided die has higher faces, so it wins more often.

explain.text: For each $f$, count the faces $s > f$: $5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14$. With 24 equally likely outcomes, $P(s > f) = \tfrac{14}{24} = \tfrac{7}{12}$.

parts.question: Using $P(s > f) = \tfrac{7}{12}$, what is $P(f > s)$? A tie counts for neither die. Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: The three events $s > f$, a tie and $f > s$ are disjoint and cover $S$: $1 - \tfrac{14}{24} - \tfrac{4}{24} = \tfrac{6}{24}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Three disjoint events cover $S$: the six-sided die higher, a tie, and the four-sided die higher.

byKey.no-ties: You took $\tfrac{7}{12}$ from 1 and left the ties in. The ties, 4 of 24, belong to neither die.
byKey.tie: That is the chance of a tie, $\tfrac{4}{24}$. Take it and $\tfrac{7}{12}$ from 1.

explain.text: The ties are $(1, 1)$ to $(4, 4)$, 4 outcomes. The three events are disjoint and cover $S$, so $P(f > s) = 1 - \tfrac{14}{24} - \tfrac{4}{24} = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

parts.question: A game pays £12 unless the four-sided die shows more, so it pays on a tie too. Using $P(f > s) = \tfrac{1}{4}$, what is its fair price, the average payout per roll?

feedback.correct: It pays £12 unless $f > s$, which has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$, so it pays on three quarters of rolls: $12 \times \tfrac{3}{4} = £9$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The game pays on every outcome except those where the four-sided die shows more.

byKey.forgot-ties: That is $12 \times \tfrac{7}{12}$, which pays only when the six-sided die wins. The game pays on a tie too.
byKey.half: You priced it as an even chance. The game pays on three quarters of rolls.
byKey.wrong-way: That is $12 \times \tfrac{1}{4}$, the price of a bet on the four-sided die. This game pays on all the other outcomes.

explain.text: The game pays £12 with chance $1 - \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{3}{4}$ and £0 otherwise. On average it pays $12 \times \tfrac{3}{4} = £9$ a roll, so £9 is the fair price.

items.prose: A fair eight-sided die, faces 1 to 8, is rolled twice. An outcome is the ordered pair $(a, b)$ of the two rolls. A stall pays a £16 prize if $A$ or $B$ happens. $A$: the first roll is 7 or more. $B$: the two rolls differ by 6 or more.

feedback.correct: Differences of 6 give $(1, 7), (2, 8)$ and differences of 7 give $(1, 8)$, each in both orders: 6 outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List the pairs that differ by 6 or by 7, in both orders.

byKey.one-order: You listed each pair once. $(1, 7)$ and $(7, 1)$ are different outcomes.
byKey.exactly-six: You counted a difference of exactly 6. A difference of 7, from 1 and 8, counts too.

explain.text: A difference of 6 needs $\{1, 7\}$ or $\{2, 8\}$, and a difference of 7 needs $\{1, 8\}$. Each pair can come in either order, so $|B| = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

parts.question: Using the 6 outcomes of $B$, how many outcomes are in $A \cap B$?

feedback.correct: Of the 6, the ones with first roll 7 or 8 are $(7, 1), (8, 2), (8, 1)$: 3 outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Go through the 6 outcomes of $B$ and keep those with $a \ge 7$.

byKey.one-order: You kept only the orders with the smaller roll first. $(7, 1)$, $(8, 2)$ and $(8, 1)$ are in $B$ too.
byKey.all-b: That is all of $B$. Keep only the outcomes whose first roll is 7 or more.

explain.text: The intersection keeps outcomes in both events. Of $B$, only $(7, 1)$, $(8, 2)$ and $(8, 1)$ start with 7 or 8, so $|A \cap B| = 3$.

parts.question: Using $|B| = 6$ and $|A \cap B| = 3$, how many outcomes are in $A \cup B$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count $A$, add $B$, then take the overlap away once.

byKey.no-overlap: You added $|A| = 16$ and $|B| = 6$. The 3 outcomes in both were counted twice.
byKey.only-a: That is $|A| = 16$ alone, or the outcomes in exactly one of the two. Add the 3 outcomes of $B$ that are not in $A$.

explain.text: $A$ has 2 choices of first roll and 8 of second, so $|A| = 16$. Adding $|B|$ counts the overlap twice, so $|A \cup B| = 16 + 6 - 3 = 19$.

parts.question: Using $|A \cup B| = 19$, what is the chance the stall pays the prize? Give an exact fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: $8 \times 8 = 64$ equally likely outcomes, 19 of them pay: $\tfrac{19}{64}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the paying outcomes by the size of the sample space.

byKey.no-overlap: That is $\tfrac{22}{64}$, with the overlap counted twice.
byKey.unordered: You divided by 36, the unordered pairs. The 64 ordered pairs are the equally likely outcomes.
byKey.sixteen: You divided by 16, the size of $A$. Divide by all 64 outcomes; a chance cannot exceed 1.

explain.text: The sample space holds $8 \times 8 = 64$ ordered pairs, all equally likely. So $P(A \cup B) = \tfrac{19}{64} \approx 0.2969$.

parts.question: Using $P(A \cup B) = \tfrac{19}{64}$, what is the fair price of one play, the average payout per play?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the prize by the chance it is paid.

byKey.no-overlap: That is $16 \times \tfrac{22}{64}$, which pays the overlap twice.
byKey.half: You priced it as an even chance. The prize is paid on 19 of 64 outcomes.
byKey.per-hit: That is the prize itself. The fair price weights it by the chance it is paid.

explain.text: The stall pays £16 with chance $\tfrac{19}{64}$ and nothing otherwise. The average payout is $16 \times \tfrac{19}{64} = £4.75$ a play.

items.prose: A desk takes prices from a primary feed and a backup feed. On any day the primary fails with chance 0.05 and the backup with chance 0.08, independently of each other and of other days. A blackout day is one where both feeds fail.

parts.question: What is the chance a given day is a blackout day? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Both feeds must fail on the same day.

byKey.added: You added the two chances. Both must fail, and for independent feeds the chances multiply.
byKey.union: That is the chance at least one feed fails. A blackout needs both.

explain.text: “Both fail” is the intersection of two independent events. Its chance is the product, $0.05 \times 0.08 = 0.004$.

parts.question: Using $P(\text{blackout}) = 0.004$, what is the chance that at least one feed works on a given day? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: “At least one works” is the complement of “both fail”: $1 - 0.004 = 0.996$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which event is the opposite of a blackout?

byKey.from-added: That is $1 - 0.13$, which follows from adding the chances in part 1. A blackout has chance 0.004.
byKey.both-work: That is $0.95 \times 0.92$, both feeds working. One working feed is enough.
byKey.same: That is the blackout chance itself. Take it from 1.

explain.text: By De Morgan, “not both fail” is “at least one works”. So the chance is $1 - 0.004 = 0.996$.

parts.question: Using $0.996$ for a day without a blackout, what is the chance of no blackout day in 20 trading days? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Every one of the 20 independent days must be free of a blackout.

byKey.linear: That is $1 - 20 \times 0.004$, which adds the daily chances. Days are independent, so multiply 0.996 twenty times.
byKey.from-both-work: That is $0.874^{20}$, every day with both feeds up. A day is safe when at least one feed works.
byKey.twenty-times: You multiplied by 20 instead of raising to the 20th power. A chance cannot exceed 1.

explain.text: Each day avoids a blackout with chance 0.996, independently. All 20 do so with chance $0.996^{20} \approx 0.9230$.

parts.question: Using $0.996^{20} \approx 0.92297$, what is the chance of at least one blackout day in the 20 days? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. “At least one blackout day” is the complement of “none”.

byKey.adding: That is $20 \times 0.004$, which counts runs with two blackout days twice. It is close here only because 0.004 is small.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no blackout day. Take it from 1.

explain.text: “At least one” is the complement of “none”. So the chance is $1 - 0.996^{20} \approx 1 - 0.92297 = 0.0770$.

items.prose: Two fair four-sided dice, faces 1 to 4, one red and one blue, are rolled together; that is one throw. A bet wins if at least one throw in a run of $n$ throws totals 8. Throws are independent.

parts.question: How many equally likely outcomes does one throw have?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pair every face of the red die with every face of the blue die.

byKey.unordered: You merged $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 1)$. The red and blue dice keep them apart, so there are 16.
byKey.added: You added the faces. Each face of the red die pairs with every face of the blue die.
byKey.totals: You counted the totals 2 to 8. They are not equally likely outcomes.

explain.text: An outcome is a pair (red, blue), and each of 4 faces pairs with each of 4. So one throw has $4 \times 4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes.

parts.question: Using the 16 outcomes, what is the chance one throw totals 8? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. List the outcomes that total 8.

byKey.totals: You gave each of the 7 totals the same chance. Only $(4, 4)$ totals 8, one outcome of 16.
byKey.unordered: That is 1 of 10, from the merged pairs. The 16 ordered pairs are the equally likely ones.

explain.text: A total of 8 needs 4 on both dice, a single outcome. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{1}{16}$ for one throw, what is the chance that no throw totals 8 in a run of 10 throws? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Each throw misses with chance $\tfrac{15}{16}$, so ten misses have chance $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^{10} \approx 0.5245$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each of the 10 independent throws must miss.

byKey.linear: That is $1 - \tfrac{10}{16}$, which adds the chances. Multiply $\tfrac{15}{16}$ ten times.
byKey.from-unordered: That is $0.9^{10}$, from the chance $\tfrac{1}{10}$. One throw totals 8 with chance $\tfrac{1}{16}$.
byKey.from-totals: That is $\left(\tfrac{6}{7}\right)^{10}$, from treating the 7 totals as equally likely.

explain.text: One throw misses 8 with chance $1 - \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{15}{16}$. The throws are independent, so all ten miss with chance $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^{10} \approx 0.5245$.

parts.question: Using $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^{10} \approx 0.52446$, what is the chance the bet wins with $n = 10$ throws? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Winning is the complement of “no throw totals 8”.

byKey.adding: That is $\tfrac{10}{16}$, which adds $\tfrac{1}{16}$ per throw. Runs with two 8s are counted twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance no throw totals 8. Take it from 1.

explain.text: The bet wins unless every throw misses. So $P(\text{win}) = 1 - 0.52446 = 0.4755$, a little under one half.

parts.question: Each throw misses with chance $\tfrac{15}{16}$, so $n$ throws all miss with chance $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^n$. What is the smallest $n$ for which the bet wins with chance above 0.9?

feedback.correct: At 36 throws, $1 - \left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^{36} \approx 0.9021$. At 35 it is 0.8955, so 36 is the first $n$ to pass 0.9.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the smallest $n$ with $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^n < 0.1$, by trying values or by taking logs.

byKey.adding: That solves $\tfrac{n}{16} > 0.9$, which adds the chances. At $n = 15$ the bet wins with chance only 0.6202.
byKey.half: That is the $n$ for a win more often than not. At $n = 11$ the chance is 0.5083, well short of 0.9.
byKey.one-short: At $n = 35$ the chance is 0.8955, just under 0.9.

explain.text: The bet wins with chance above 0.9 when $\left(\tfrac{15}{16}\right)^n < 0.1$. Taking logs, $n > \tfrac{\ln 0.1}{\ln (15/16)} \approx 35.7$, so the smallest $n$ is 36.
